blocks.text: [II, 647] Moreover, others also mention the hunter partridge. Except that instead of "hunter" Athenaeus, book 9, calls it θηρεύοντα πέρδικα [thēreuonta perdika], a hunting partridge. Pliny ^{a)} calls it the fowler's informer, or rather his decoy [illicem], as Turnebus ^{b)} and Scaliger ^{c)} advise reading. Aelian ^{d)}, in the same sense, says τὸν παλεύοντα πέρδικα [ton paleuonta perdika]. Eustathius of Antioch says τὸν πέρδικα συμπράττοντα τοῖς θηρευταῖς πρὸς τὴν ἄγραν [ton perdika sympratonta tois thēreutais pros tēn agran]. Theodoret, in the Catena on Jeremiah, says πέρδικα θηρατικὸν [perdika thēratikon], adding that such birds are obtained from Babylon. Indeed, this kind of fowling was already in use in the East long ago. Accordingly, in Xenophon, book 1 of the Cyropaedia, Cambyses addresses his son Cyrus thus: Ὄρνιθες δὲ ἐπεπαίδευτό σοι, ὥς τέ σοι μὲν τὰ συμφέροντα ὑπερητεῖν, τὰς δὲ ὁμοφύλους ὄρνιθας ἐξαπατᾷν [Ornithes de epepaideuto soi, hōs te soi men ta sympheronta hypērētein, tas de homophylous ornithas exapatan], "You had trained birds so that they would both serve you in what was useful and deceive birds of the same kind." Whoever wants more on this subject should consult those we have cited. Also Albertus Magnus, where he treats of the cubeth ^{e)}, that is, the female partridge, [col. 91] in Arabic القبج [al-qabj], which he says, when shut in a cage, lures the males to itself. Damir, however, attributes this very thing to the male in these words: في طبع الذكر ان يخدع امثاله بقرقرته ولهذا اتخذه الصيادون في اشراكهم ليكثر القرقرة فيجتمع الحجل فيقعن معه [fī ṭabʿ al-dhakar an yakhdaʿa amthālahu bi-qarqaratihi wa-li-hādhā ittakhadhahu al-ṣayyādūn fī ashrākihim li-yukthira al-qarqara fa-yajtamiʿa al-ḥajal fa-yaqaʿna maʿahu] "It is the nature of the male to lure birds like itself by its call; therefore hunters take it with them, so that by its frequent calling it may gather the female partridges, which fly to it." But that both sexes are used for this, with varying success, is shown at length by the Philosopher, Aelian and Athenaeus in the places cited above. The Arabic version of Sirach, instead of القبج في القفص [al-qabj fī al-qafaṣ] a partridge in a cage, has, without any sense, الصنج في الرقص [al-ṣanj fī al-raqṣ] a sistrum, or a cymbal in the dance. That this arose through the ignorance of scribes is shown by the similarity of the letters. For Pagnino, Castalio, Arias, Camerarius, Jansenius and others, πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς [perdix thēreutēs] is a captured partridge, as though it were πέρδιξ θηρευθεὶς [perdix thēreutheis]. By the same error the Syriac has ܐܝܟ ܩܩܒܢܐ ܕܨܝܕܐ like a partridge taken in hunting; and the Vulgate, "as a partridge is led into the cage."
